fields.Text: The two core functional requirements of a URL shortener are: {{c1::generate a unique short URL for a given long URL}} and {{c2::redirect a short URL to its original long URL}}.
Non-functional requirements for a URL shortener include {{c1::high availability}}, {{c2::low latency redirection}}, and {{c3::the short URL should not be easily predictable/guessable}}.

The high-level architecture of a URL shortener typically includes: {{c1::a load balancer}}, {{c2::stateless application servers}}, {{c3::a key-value store for URL mappings}}, and {{c4::a cache layer (e.g. Redis) in front of the database}}.

Key scaling bottlenecks in a URL shortener and their fixes: {{c1::hot-key read traffic}} is fixed by {{c2::a caching layer (e.g. Redis) plus CDN edge caching}}; {{c3::a single ID-generation service becoming a bottleneck}} is fixed by {{c4::pre-allocating ID ranges per server or using a distributed ID generator like Snowflake}}.

fields.Front: Should short URLs in a URL shortener system expire?
fields.Back: Optionally yes — support a configurable expiration/TTL per link, after which the short link becomes invalid.

fields.Front: Why must a URL shortener prioritize availability over strong consistency?
fields.Back: Redirects are on the critical read path for every click; an outage breaks all shared links, so the system favors AP (availability) in the CAP tradeoff, tolerating brief staleness of newly created links across replicas.

fields.Front: In a typical URL shortener capacity estimate, if there are 100M new URLs created per month, what is the approximate write QPS?
If the read:write ratio for a URL shortener is 100:1 and write QPS is ~40, what is the approximate read QPS?
Estimate storage needed for 100M URLs/month over 5 years if each record is ~500 bytes.
Write the REST endpoint to create a short URL, given a long URL and optional custom alias/expiration.
Write the REST endpoint used to redirect a short URL to its long URL.
Should the redirect endpoint use a 301 or 302 HTTP status, and why does it matter?
fields.Back: 302 (temporary redirect) is generally preferred — it keeps every click hitting the server for analytics. 301 (permanent) lets browsers cache the redirect, saving server load but losing per-click analytics.

fields.Front: Write a minimal schema for the urls table in a URL shortener.
fields.Back:
urls(
  short_code VARCHAR(7) PRIMARY KEY,
  long_url   TEXT NOT NULL,
  user_id    BIGINT,
  created_at TIMESTAMP,
  expires_at TIMESTAMP NULL
)

fields.Front: Why is a key-value store (e.g. DynamoDB/Cassandra) often preferred over a relational DB for the URL mapping table?
fields.Back: The access pattern is a simple key lookup (short_code → long_url) at huge read scale with no complex joins/transactions needed, so a KV store scales horizontally more easily and cheaply than a relational DB.

fields.Front: Why add a cache (e.g. Redis) in front of the URL mapping database?
fields.Back: Redirect traffic follows a hot-key distribution — a small percentage of URLs get most of the clicks — so caching hot mappings drastically cuts database read load and latency.

fields.Front: What alphabet does base62 encoding use for short URL codes?
How many unique short codes does a 7-character base62 string provide?
Describe the counter + base62 approach to generating short URLs.
fields.Back: Maintain a globally unique, monotonically increasing counter (e.g. via a distributed ID generator or a DB auto-increment range), then base62-encode the counter value to produce the short code — this guarantees uniqueness with no collision checking needed.

fields.Front: What is a drawback of using a simple auto-increment counter for short codes, and how is it mitigated?
fields.Back: Sequential codes are predictable/guessable, letting users enumerate all URLs. Mitigate by pre-shuffling the ID space (e.g. a random permutation, or hashing the counter before encoding) so codes appear random while staying unique.

fields.Front: Describe the alternative hash-based (MD5/SHA + truncate) approach to generating short codes, and its main problem.
fields.Back: Hash the long URL (e.g. MD5), base62-encode it, and take the first 7 characters. Problem: truncated hashes can collide, so you must check the DB for an existing code and retry with a salt/suffix on collision.

fields.Front: How can the database layer be scaled once a single instance can't handle URL mapping read volume?
fields.Back: Horizontally shard the key-value store (e.g. by a hash of short_code) and add read replicas, so reads are distributed across many nodes.

fields.Front: What is the main tradeoff when choosing a 301 (permanent) redirect over a 302 for short links?
fields.Back: 301 improves performance (browsers cache it, reducing server hits) but sacrifices the ability to track every click for analytics, since cached redirects never reach the server again.
